name: PT Pollux Hotels Group Tbk

frontmatter.title: Pollux Hotels Group — a Semarang mall-and-hotel landlord priced for a developer's winter
frontmatter.summary: Pollux owns five malls and five hotels in Semarang, Batam and Cikarang, with a small apartment developer on top, financed by debt the market prices and equity it does not. Recurring income is the majority of gross profit and the reason the company survived the last cycle. Our gross asset value per share is above the price, but the discount a controlled, undividended and illiquid register justifies takes our value below it, and no dividend is paid. Initiate at Sell.
thesis: Recurring income carries the business: malls, hotels and building management produced the majority of revenue and gross profit in every year the company discloses by segment, while the developer arm is a handover cycle, not an annuity.

The capital structure sets the share price: net debt is several multiples of EBITDA and interest absorbs most of operating profit, so value moves with refinancing and the policy rate rather than with presales.

Gross RNAV per share is above the traded price, but the target discount the peer band justifies takes our value below it, and a thin float and tiny daily turnover mean the gap is not arbitrable inside twelve months.

Operations are improving — global hotel operators, serviced-apartment conversions, a CGIF-guaranteed sustainability bond — yet none of that puts cash in the hands of minority holders while the payout stays at zero.
We turn constructive when recurring income clearly covers interest and a dividend policy exists; we turn negative if the Batam handover cycle stalls with debt still at our multiple.

blocks.text: **Sell. Target Rp487, -28.4% total return from Rp680.** Pollux Hotels Group is not a land-bank story. It is a Semarang-based owner of five malls, five hotels and a building-management business, with an apartment developer bolted on whose revenue arrives in lumps when a tower is handed over [S2]. The recurring businesses — mall rent, hotel rooms and management fees — produced the majority of gross profit in every period the company discloses, and their gross margin has held in the low fifties [S2]. The developer segment produced a sixth of revenue in one full year and half of it in the next five-month period, which is what makes reported earnings so unstable and the market so unwilling to capitalise them [S2].

The valuation we can evidence is asset-based. Our RNAV method puts the shares at Rp435 after the target discount, against a traded Rp680; the two cross-checks run above it, at Rp769 on our forward earnings multiple of 23.6 and Rp852 on book at 0.8 [S2]. The three-method blend is a weighted average — 60% of Rp435 plus 20% of Rp769 plus 20% of Rp852, which is Rp585 today — and that blend, not a scenario number, is what feeds the scenario set. The probability-weighted twelve-month value across our bear, base and bull cases is Rp695, and Rp487 after the liquidity adjustment the engine applies to an illiquid name. The 30% liquidity haircut is the most honest number in this report: insiders hold 80.0% of the register, the free float is 20.0%, institutional ownership is 0.0% and three-month turnover averages IDR78.1m a day (data pack). A discount that wide cannot be arbitraged by anybody who needs to build a position.

Our variant view against a market that has marked the shares from 1,955.0 down to 655.0 is that the operating business is not deteriorating. During 2026 the company signed or extended hotel agreements with Marriott International, The Ascott Limited, Accor and Wyndham Hotels & Resorts, is converting apartment towers into serviced apartments, and had already issued the first sustainability-linked bond in Indonesian hospitality, certified idAAAcg and guaranteed by the Asian Development Bank's CGIF trust fund [S3][S5][S6]. What has not changed is the arithmetic of the balance sheet: net debt of IDR1,352.0bn against EBITDA of IDR187.4bn — 7.2 times on the data pack's un-restated FY2025A depreciation line, and 4.9 times in FY2026E on the restated basis that carries the audited D&A charge, so the restated FY2025A multiple sits between the two [S4] — interest expense of IDR105.4bn on profit before tax of IDR92.5bn, and no dividend declared in any year of the available history (data pack). The equity is an option on cheaper money, and options on leverage do not re-rate on operational press releases.

Three variables move the value. First, the rate path: our cost of equity is 16.6% and WACC 12.0%, built off an unlevered beta of 0.90 and a levered 1.61; a company with more than half its capital structure in bank and bond debt is a rates instrument whatever management says [S2]. Second, the handover schedule: IDR552.0bn of customer advances sat on the balance sheet at the end of May 2025, down from the year-end figure, and it is the best evidence we have on the handover pipeline - not a forward backlog, because no later balance is in the archive [S2 p.21]. Third, the discount itself: at 45.0% we already assume the market keeps most of its haircut, so the return depends on that narrowing, not on the assets appreciating.

Indonesian listed developers have traded below appraised net asset value for most of the past decade. The discount reflects the distance between an appraisal and a cash flow: land is illiquid, handovers slip, and the controlling family decides when value is realised and whether it is distributed. Family-controlled developers in secondary cities carry an additional haircut because the float is thin, the free-float requirement is met rather than exceeded, and index deletions remove the marginal institutional buyer. None of this is specific to Pollux; the point is that a wide discount is the normal state of these securities, not an anomaly waiting to be corrected.

Pollux was incorporated in 2009, listed as PT Pollux Investasi Internasional and renamed PT Pollux Hotels Group in 2021. Its registered office is in Mega Kuningan in Jakarta; its operating office is on the fourth floor of the Paragon Mall on Jl. Pemuda in Semarang [S2]. It reports four operating segments — Mall, Developer, Hotel and Administrator — and employed 653.0 people at the last count (data pack). The president director is Lie Jemmy and the finance director Maria Indah Pratiwi (data pack); the group's public-facing figure in the bond and award coverage is Handojo K. Setyadi [S5][S6].

**The portfolio is fourteen named operating projects.** The company's own project table lists Paragon Mall in Semarang (operating since 2010), the five-star Po Hotel Semarang (2012), the W/R Simpang Lima apartments and Louis Kienne Simpang Lima hotel (2016), The Pinnacle apartments and Louis Kienne Pandanaran hotel (2017), Pollux Mall Central City in Semarang (2009), the Louis Kienne Pemuda hotel and Marquis de Lafayette apartments (2018), the Louis Kienne Resort Bandungan, the Louis Kienne Resort Senggigi in Lombok (2018), Pollux Mall Chadstone on the Cikarang–Cibarusah road in Bekasi regency, opened 23 February 2023, and the Meisterstadt apartments and Pollux Mall Batam at Batam Center (2019) [S2]. The income core is five malls with roughly 90.0 thousand square metres of net lettable area and five hotels with about 850 rooms [S2]. Two entities carry most of this: PT Cakrawala Sakti Kencana for Paragon Mall and Po Hotel, PT Graha Masindo Pratama and PT Pahala Agung for the Pandanaran and Pemuda assets, PT Bumi Pasifik Kencana for Chadstone, and PT Pollux Barelang Mega Superblok for Batam [S2].

**Segment mix.** In FY2024, the last full year disclosed by segment, malls produced IDR218.8bn of revenue and IDR104.2bn of gross profit; hotels IDR139.1bn and IDR82.1bn; the administrator IDR45.6bn and IDR24.3bn; and the developer IDR83.1bn and IDR31.2bn [S2]. That makes a recurring block of IDR403.5bn of revenue against IDR83.1bn of development revenue, with a recurring gross margin above fifty per cent and a developer margin in the high thirties [S2]. In the five months to May 2025 the mix inverted: developer revenue alone reached IDR196.3bn as Batam apartments were handed over, against IDR15.1bn for the whole of FY2023 [S2]. Management frames the balance as deliberate — its stated strategy is to balance recurring income against sales income and to stay focused on integrated superblocks and integrated townships [S2].

**How it sells and builds.** Sales run through a direct force of sales executives plus agent networks: the company describes a Pollux National Network of lead agents spanning 15 provinces, supported by thousands of agents, with a customer database in the thousands, and promotion across broadcast, print, online and property exhibitions [S2]. Construction is contracted at a fixed price with a main contractor for each whole project, which the company presents as eliminating exposure to steel and cement price moves [S2]. That transfers input risk but concentrates completion risk, and completion timing is precisely what determines when developer revenue is recognised.

**Where the product goes.** The customer base is middle-income households in the catchment cities plus, in Batam, expatriate tenants: the company has been explicit that its Fraser Residence product targets expatriates from China and Korea working in the Batam industrial zones [S5]. For 2026 the company marketed Chadstone apartments (about 70.0% sold at the time of the prospectus), Meisterstadt apartments and shophouses, Gangnam District apartments and pre-sale units at Pollux Technopolis, and says it will extend to Bekasi and Karawang and to other cities with growing middle-income populations and tourism destinations [S2].

**Position.** Pollux is a local incumbent rather than a national developer. In Semarang the Paragon Mall is the established mixed-use anchor and, by the company's own account and the rating agency's, the largest single contributor to revenue [S2]. In Cikarang the Chadstone asset serves a factory-employment catchment. In Batam the superblock was acquired rather than developed: the 2024 purchase of PT Cemerlang Sentosa Mulia, owner of PT Pollux Barelang Megasuperblok, added inventory of 88.2% in a single year and reclassified customer advances into investment property, lifting net investment properties by 78.4% in the same year [S2]. Against CTRA, PWON or SMRA, Pollux has no national platform, no listed vehicle for its recurring income and a fraction of the balance sheet.

**Group and control.** Insiders hold 80.0% and the free float is 20.0% (data pack, IDX registry). The FY2023 accounts name the related parties: PT Rockfields Properti Indonesia and PT World Apparel as entities under common control, PT Golden Flower and PT Graha Lestari Internusa as counterparties of trade receivables, and PT Bank Perkreditan Rakyat Pollux, a rural bank sharing key management personnel, which holds the group's cash and provides consumer financing [S4]. The disclosed balances were immaterial against total assets of trillions of rupiah [S4] — the flag is structural, not quantified.

**Size and growth.** The company's own bond document, summarising the sector view it took to the market, notes that property and real estate still contribute roughly 6.5 to 7.0 per cent of domestic and foreign direct investment in Indonesia, that participants entered 2025 optimistic but facing softening middle-class purchasing power, rising land prices and rate normalisation, and that the offsets expected were tax incentives, the new-capital build and urban housing demand [S2]. That describes Pollux's market precisely: product is mortgage-financed apartments in secondary cities, land is the inflating input, and policy support arrives as a tax concession rather than as price.

**The drivers that matter here.** Three. The policy rate, because apartment buyers finance and the company refinances: the house macro deck puts the BI rate at 5.8% in 2027 against a spot of the same level, and the model's cost of debt is 8.5% on opening debt (data pack) [S2]. Local demand in Semarang, Batam and Cikarang, which for hotels is a function of industrial and government travel and, in Batam, of Singapore and expatriate traffic [S5]. And the rupiah, not because Pollux earns foreign currency but because imported construction inflation and a defensive central bank travel together: our deck has USD/IDR at 18,350 in 2027 (macro deck).

**Regulation and tax.** Pollux pays both a current corporate charge and final tax on property sales, visible in the income statement lines of the prospectus [S2]; the blended effective rate in our model is 27.8% because final tax bites hardest in the years when developer revenue is recognised. The bond is issued under a sustainability-linked framework with an external verification arrangement and KPI reporting in the annual and sustainability report [S2]. Mortgage rules, acquisition property tax and the periodic incentive packages are the levers that move demand for the company's product; none of them is in the company's gift.

**Competitive position and moat.** The moat is incumbency and location, not brand or scale. The rating agency's asset-quality rationale is the clearest external statement of it: most assets sit in Semarang, Batam and Cikarang close to public facilities, and Paragon Mall is the largest revenue contributor [S2]. The causal link to the mixed-use concept is our reading, not the agency's wording. That is a genuine local monopoly of convenience, and it is also the limit of the moat: the same asset cannot be replicated in another city, which is why the growth plan is serviced apartments and operator agreements rather than new malls.

**Five forces.** Rivalry in apartments is high and local — the alternative to a Pollux unit is a completed secondary unit at a lower effective price. Rivalry in malls is moderate because each catchment supports few centres. Buyer power is rising: apartment purchases are deferred by rate cycles and by the memory of projects that handed over late. Supplier power has been contracted away at the project level through fixed-price main contracts, which moves the risk to contractor solvency and completion timing [S2]. Substitutes are landed houses and shophouses, still the default Indonesian purchase, which caps the pricing power of a high-rise product. Barriers to entry are land, permits and capital, which protects the incumbent mall and the incumbent's cheap legacy land.

**Peer and external read.** The company's own rating rationale expects recurring income above half of the total, gross margin around 50.0% and EBITDA margin around 45.0%, with debt to EBITDA averaging about 4.6 times across 2025 and 2026 [S2]. Our forecast puts EBITDA margin at 41.4% and net debt to EBITDA at 4.9 times in FY2026E: the margin is close to the agency's number once depreciation is restated to the level the audited notes show, and the leverage ratio is above the agency's 4.6 times because the data pack's depreciation understates EBITDA and because the IDR100.0bn early repayment of the BNI facility does not reduce gross debt to zero [S4][S8].

Secondary-city Indonesian malls have held occupancy better than prime Jakarta retail since the pandemic, because the catchment has fewer competing centres and the tenant mix leans to necessity spending rather than discretionary fashion. Hotels outside Bali and Jakarta recovered later and remain rate-constrained, and under an operator agreement the owner keeps the asset risk while the brand captures the demand upside in fees. A developer that owns both the mall and the hotel in the same superblock is effectively selling the same local customer base twice, which is good for occupancy and bad for negotiating leverage with any single tenant.

**The reported history.** Revenue went from IDR330.5bn in FY2022 to IDR360.9bn, IDR486.6bn and IDR615.6bn in FY2025 — 26.5% growth in the last year alone (data pack). That growth is not organic rent growth: it is the developer segment clearing apartments in Batam and Cikarang, which is why the gross margin fell from 49.7% to 45.8% as lower-margin handovers displaced rental income in the mix (data pack). The company's own five-month comparison makes the mechanism explicit: revenue up 104.9% year on year, driven by the developer segment [S2].

**What the data pack gets wrong, and how we restate it.** Indonesian statements use the direct cash-flow method and the data pack's depreciation line is a fraction of the real charge. For FY2023 the pack carries D&A of IDR39.5bn; the audited notes show depreciation of investment properties of IDR39.5bn and a further IDR18.6bn of fixed-asset depreciation charged to cost of revenue and G&A [S4]. Our FY2023A EBITDA of IDR145.0bn adds back only the investment-property line, so it sits below the 45.0% margin the company's own rating rationale expects for the business [S2]: the engine's EBITDA is EBIT plus D&A, and the add-back we can source for FY2023 is the smaller of the two audited charges. The pack's FY2024 and FY2025 D&A lines are smaller again — IDR10.1bn and IDR10.3bn on revenue of IDR615.6bn — so the 30.5% margin the pack shows is an artefact of the add-back, not of the business. At the IDR39.5bn investment-property plus IDR18.6bn fixed-asset charge the audited notes show, the restated actual closes most of the gap to our FY2026E forecast of 41.4%, and we read that narrowing as the restatement doing its job rather than as independent confirmation of the forecast: the forecast margin is the recurring block's 52.0% gross margin less opex held at the last actual's ratio, so restoring the actual's true D&A moves the two onto one accounting basis. The residual is mix — the higher-margin recurring block growing faster than the developer — not a margin the company has never earned. For the forecast we carry 9.4% of revenue for depreciation and hold it through FY2030E, the same rate the audited FY2023 charge implies on last year's revenue, because no archived source shows either depreciation pool running off.

**Revenue build.** We split revenue into the recurring block (mall, hotel and management) and the developer. The recurring block was IDR403.5bn of revenue in FY2024 with a gross margin of 52.0% [S2]; we grow it at 6.0% in FY2026E, then 7.0% and 6.0% through the forecast, and hold the gross margin at 52.0% [S2]. The developer is modelled as the recognised handover flow — IDR83.1bn in FY2024, IDR196.3bn in five months of 2025 — growing at 15.0% in FY2026E off the IDR552.0bn customer-advance backlog, at a gross margin of 43.0% [S2]. Our FY2025A split is derived rather than disclosed: the company published no full-year segment table in the sources we could archive, so we grossed the five-month segment figures up at their FY2024 five-month share of the year, which reconciles to the pack's FY2025 revenue of IDR615.6bn and gives IDR419.3bn recurring against IDR196.3bn development. The report states that derivation openly because it is an estimate, not a quote: no audited FY2025 segment note exists in the archive, the half-year 2026 filings we hold carry consolidated revenue only, so the mix cannot be re-based on actuals. The direction of the error is knowable - the Batam handover peaked in the first half of 2025, so a five-month share overstates the developer block - which is why we do not let the derived mix carry more than the closing-year growth rate.

**Costs.** The biggest fixed cost is not in the income statement as a line: it is interest. Operating costs are modest — general and administrative expense of IDR101.5bn in FY2024 on revenue of IDR486.6bn, falling to IDR35.6bn on IDR306.8bn in the five months to May 2025 as the developer revenue scaled [S2]. We hold SG&A at 17.0% of revenue through the forecast, the ratio the last full actual year (FY2025A) earns on IDR104.8bn of operating cost against IDR615.6bn of revenue (data pack). The higher FY2024 ratio is the pre-handover cost base of a year with far less developer revenue, plus other operating expenses the filing shows separately [S2 p.22]; holding the last actual, not the five-month ratio, is the most likely path because head-office cost is quasi-fixed. Interest expense was IDR105.4bn in FY2025; at a cost of debt of 8.5% on opening debt it stays in that range for the forecast years unless the company refinances, and the December 2025 bond — IDR55.0bn of three-year at 5.8% and IDR445.0bn of five-year at 6.2%, CGIF-guaranteed — was priced at or below the bank cost it replaced [S6].

**Cash flow and working capital.** Operating cash flow was negative in FY2025 (IDR-52.2bn free cash flow after a working-capital swing of IDR181.7bn) because the Batam handovers consumed inventory and customer advances unwound (data pack). This is the normal shape of a developer's cash flow at the top of a handover cycle and not, by itself, an earnings-quality flag. What is an earnings-quality question is the size of the advance liability: IDR552.0bn of customer advances at 31 May 2025 against revenue of IDR615.6bn means the company had already been paid for a substantial part of the next two years of handovers, which de-risks the revenue but also means the cash has been spent on construction [S0][S2].

**Balance sheet.** Total liabilities were IDR2,199.4bn at 31 May 2025 against parent equity of IDR2,071.8bn [S2], a debt-to-equity ratio of about one times that the company reports as 1.05 times [S2]. Investment properties carried IDR1,675.6bn net and inventories IDR1,074.9bn [S2]. The bank debt was IDR1,298.5bn non-current at that date [S2], plus a small current portion. Net debt is IDR1,352.0bn against EBITDA of IDR187.4bn, or 7.2 times on the data pack's FY2025A D&A line of IDR10.3bn — an un-restated number and the only FY2025A multiple the pack supports. On the charge the audited notes show — IDR39.5bn of investment-property depreciation plus IDR18.6bn of fixed-asset depreciation [S4] — FY2025A net debt sits over EBIT of IDR177.1bn plus that charge, which restates the last actual to a multiple above the forecast's and below the pack's. Our FY2026E forecast carries the same charge at 9.4% of revenue, and there net debt of IDR1,360.7bn is 4.9 times EBITDA in FY2026E; that is the forecast multiple this report relies on — high for a property owner and the central fact of this report. Interest cover from recurring gross profit is adequate; interest cover from net profit is not.

**Capital allocation.** No dividend has been declared since at least FY2022 (data pack). The bond proceeds refinanced bank debt and fund solar installations, and the BNI facility financed two West Java hotels, one of which the company repaid IDR100.0bn of early in November 2025 to "improve the financial structure" [S6][S8]. The pattern is reinvestment ahead of distribution, which is defensible while the recurring base is being converted to serviced apartments, and indefensible if it continues after that conversion is complete.

**Forecast.** We forecast revenue of IDR670.2bn in FY2026E, EBITDA of IDR277.2bn and net profit to parent of IDR71.4bn, rising to IDR772.2bn and IDR318.7bn by FY2028E. EPS of Rp35.5 on 2,011 million shares is what the market is paying 19.2 times for at Rp680 (data pack multiples). The forecasts carry no dividend, so the value is entirely in the assets and in what a future buyer of those assets would pay [S0][S8].

**Why RNAV is the primary method.** A property developer's earnings describe handovers that were contracted two years earlier, and Pollux's earnings swing with the mix between a rental block earning a 52.0% gross margin and an apartment block at 43.0% [S2]. Discounting those earnings at a cost of equity of 16.6% would capitalise a handover accident. What the company owns is more stable than what it reports: five malls, five hotels, land and apartments under construction, and a stake in associates carried at IDR505.8bn [S2]. So RNAV carries 60% of the weight, with earnings at 20% and book at 20% as cross-checks on whether the asset value is reachable.

**The RNAV build.** We date the balance-sheet legs — net debt, cash, minorities, the associate and the land leg — to 30 June 2026, the balance-sheet date the engine uses (the bridge net-debt line is that 30 June 2026 figure; it stands above the FY2025A model line at 31 December 2025 only by the cash movement since the year end — a date difference, not a reconciling item — and the two are not additive). The investment-property leg is not a balance-sheet line: it is a capitalisation of forecast recurring gross profit, and the IDR1,675.6bn at which the properties are carried at 31 May 2025 is the book reference that capitalisation has to clear, not a June 2026 asset. We take the land leg from the inventory line on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, then deduct the associate over-carry inside the same leg so a related party carried far above its evidenced value is not paid for twice [S4 p.59; our house RNAV for that entity]. The IDR1,074.9bn of inventories in the sustainable-bond prospectus is the last audited figure we can quote, dated 31 May 2025 [S2 p.21]: it is the reference for what the land leg contains, not the number we use, because pairing a May 2025 asset figure with June 2026 net debt would debit the equity for a year of interest it never paid. We apply no uplift on top — the carrying amount is already the audited lower of cost and net realisable value, and raw land far from infrastructure is not a ready township. For the Batam superblock leg the consideration paid for PT Cemerlang Sentosa Mulia and its ownership terms are not disclosed anywhere in the archive, so that leg's cost basis is unverified as well as un-uplifted: a second reason not to add an appraisal premium, and a number to ask management for [S2]. We capitalise recurring GROSS profit - mall, hotel and management revenue less its direct cost, the line the segment note discloses margins on - at a gross-profit yield of 13.0%. That yield capitalises our forecast recurring gross profit to more than the IDR1,675.6bn at which the investment properties are carried, so it does not undercut carrying value on the forecast; on the audited FY2024A recurring gross profit the same yield capitalises to slightly less than book, which is exactly why we treat the cap rate as the largest single lever in the RNAV rather than as a value with a margin of safety [S2 p.32]. The rate is not a peer cap rate: because the denominator is gross profit, it embeds the G&A, property-tax and operator-fee load the segment table keeps below the line, and it is therefore higher than a net-income yield on the same assets.

**The associates line.** The investments line on the latest balance sheet is not a portfolio: the FY2023 accounts name it as an equity-method stake of just over a quarter of PT Rockfields Properti Indonesia, an entity under common control, carried at acquisition cost plus equity pickup, with a de minimis Fair-Value-Model residual in PT Knightsbridge Luxury Development [S4 p.59]. Our own published coverage of Rockfields values its equity at a house RNAV per share on its issued shares, which makes the stake worth roughly a quarter of the IDR505.8bn the balance sheet carries it at: the strongest evidence in the archive says the carrying amount is several times the value of the underlying equity. We make that deduction in the valuation bridge, where the engine applies it to the earnings and book cross-checks, and carry the same adjustment inside the RNAV net asset basis so the asset total is not counted twice. After the 45.0% target discount the method produces Rp435 per share against a traded Rp680.

**The discount.** IDX developers trade at persistent, wide discounts to RNAV, and our own published coverage of the peer set runs from the high twenties to the high eighties with most names in the fifties and sixties. The discount prices float, control and distribution rather than the asset basis: Pollux has a free float of 20.0%, no institutional ownership, 80.0% insider control and no dividend in any archived year (data pack). We use 45.0%, the lower-quartile end of that band, because our RNAV refuses any uplift on the land bank and capitalises recurring income on a gross-profit yield; there is no dated realisation event - no REIT, no asset sale, no dividend policy - that would justify a narrower discount. The bear tests the wider band.

**WACC and cost of equity.** The build is in the table: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%; an unlevered beta of 0.90, levered to 1.61 at a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.01 and a 22.0% tax rate; a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%; weights of 49.9% equity and 50.1% debt. That gives a cost of equity of 16.6% and a WACC of 12.0%. The beta is the number to argue about: a developer with half its capital structure in debt and a thin float should have a high beta, and 1.61 is high; the counter-argument is that the real risk here is idiosyncratic leverage rather than market correlation, and that a beta fitted to a stock that has halved in a year is fitted to the collapse. We leave it where the house deck puts it and note the sensitivity.

**Target construction, step by step.** Three separately computed methods are weighted into one blended value, and the arithmetic is shown so a reader can check it rather than take it: 60% × Rp435 + 20% × Rp769 + 20% × Rp852 = Rp585, where the products of the rounded per-share figures fall a fraction under the blend because each leg is rounded to the rupiah. That blend is today's value; the base scenario applies no shocks, so the base case's value today is the blend itself and its twelve-month target is that value rolled forward one year at the cost of equity, Rp682. The bear target is Rp574 at a 25% probability and the bull Rp842 at 25%, around the base at 50%, so the probability-weighted twelve-month value is Rp695. That scenario-weighted figure is a different number from the method blend, built from different inputs — the blend answers "what is the business worth on our methods today", the scenario-weighted figure answers "what will the market pay in twelve months across the paths we think possible". The 30% illiquidity discount, applied to the scenario-weighted figure and not to each method, gives the published target of Rp487, a -28.4% return from Rp680. Those are two different haircuts and the reader should not net them: the 45.0% RNAV discount prices the asset basis and the control risk over it — land that is not for sale, a family that decides when value is realised — while the 30% is an execution haircut for a register whose turnover cannot absorb an exit. Strip the execution haircut out and the target is the probability-weighted Rp695, a return close to flat against Rp680; the SELL therefore rests on the liquidity adjustment, not on the asset discount alone. The chain runs blend Rp585 to base target Rp682 to scenario-weighted Rp695 to published Rp487; nothing in it is a target multiple borrowed from the market.

**Cross-checks and what their divergence tells us.** The P/E value is Rp769 on a forward multiple of 23.6 times, 76.7% above RNAV and the P/BV value is Rp852 at 0.8 times, 95.7% above. Both cross-checks sit well over the asset method, and the divergence is explainable rather than fatal: the earnings and book bridges deduct the associate over-carry separately, both capitalise a balance sheet whose investment properties stand near cost, and neither applies the RNAV discount or the liquidity haircut. The asset method is therefore the conservative one, and the discount - not the asset value - is what the market is pricing. That is why the 60% RNAV / 20% earnings / 20% book weighting gives Rp585 and not a higher figure.

The sensitivity table moves the RNAV discount against presales growth. The discount registers; the presales path does not move our asset-based value at all, which is the point of the method and the reason a handover miss cannot be valued through the assets. That is a feature of the valuation and a defect of the strategy: it is why no handover risk reaches the target, and it is why the bear case now shocks the two inputs that do carry it - the gross-profit yield and the discount - instead of the developer line alone.

**The house-card checks, in one place.** Land bank: the land leg of the RNAV is the inventory line on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet (data pack, unaudited) less the associate over-carry, which is deducted inside that same leg; it is not the IDR1,074.9bn of inventories dated 31 May 2025, which is the last audited figure we can quote and the reference for what that leg contains [S2 p.21]. We apply no uplift, so an appraisal above carrying value would be promoter arithmetic [S2]. Presales: the pipeline KPI is customer advances, IDR552.0bn at 31 May 2025, which is what the FY2026-FY2027 handovers draw on; underwriting that backlog below the base case is the bear case, not the base [S2]. Mix: the developer is the minority of revenue and the recurring block the majority, so a presales miss moves value by a few per cent rather than by the share of the mix a presales-led developer would carry [S2]. Discount versus own band: the shares trade below book, consistent with the five-year price-to-book history (data pack history), which is why we use an asset method and a 30% liquidity haircut rather than a target multiple. Catalyst: the 2026 hotel completions and the 2028 Series A refinancing are the two dated events that could narrow the discount [S6][S8]. Gearing and currency: net debt of IDR1,352.0bn is 7.2 times the data pack's un-restated FY2025A EBITDA of IDR187.4bn and 4.9 times in FY2026E on the restated charge the audited notes support [S4], and interest of IDR105.4bn consumes most of a IDR92.5bn pre-tax profit; the archived balance sheet shows rupiah bank debt and the rupiah bond, with no foreign-currency facility disclosed [S2][S6]. BI path: 5.8% in 2027, held flat, is the mortgage-rate assumption the whole forecast keys off (macro deck).

**What the price implies.** At Rp680 the market is valuing the equity at IDR1,367.2bn, which is less than the carried value of the malls and hotels plus the associates stake, before any value is given to the land and construction leg, which we carry at the inventory line less the associate over-carry rather than at the gross inventory [S2 p.21; S4 p.59]. Read the other way, the price implies a cap rate well above our 13.0% on recurring gross profit, or a discount to RNAV wider than 45.0%, or both. The implied value of the recurring block, after deducting net debt and adding nothing for the developer, is the test we would ask a bull to pass: at Rp680 the market is paying book for the developer and a discount for the income.

**Leverage and refinancing (likelihood high, impact high).** Net debt is IDR1,352.0bn against EBITDA of IDR187.4bn (7.2 times on the data pack's un-restated FY2025A depreciation, 4.9 times in FY2026E once the audited D&A charge is restored [S4]) and interest of IDR105.4bn absorbs most of profit before tax of IDR92.5bn (data pack). The IDR500.0bn bond, Series A at three years and Series B at five, removed the near-term maturity wall and the CGIF guarantee lowered the coupon, but the IDR445.0bn Series B is a bullet [S6]. A property company that cannot refinance does not get to argue about NAV.

**Rate transmission (likelihood medium, impact high).** Apartment demand and the cost of the company's own debt both key off the policy rate, so a hold-higher cycle hits volume and margin simultaneously. Our base case has the BI rate at 5.8% in 2027 (macro deck); each point above that is a cost to the recurring business and a tax on buyers.

**Handover execution (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Developer revenue is recognised on handover, so a slipped tower moves a year of earnings. The backlog of IDR552.0bn customer advances at 31 May 2025 is the mitigant [S2], and the two West Java hotels at 85.0% construction in November 2025 are the visible pipeline [S8].

**Governance and control (likelihood medium, impact medium).** Insiders hold 80.0% with a 20.0% float (data pack). Related parties include entities under common control and a rural bank sharing key management, and the 2024 Batam acquisition came from outside the group but reclassified customer advances into investment property, which changes how the asset base looks without adding cash [S2][S4]. Family control is not a reason to avoid the shares by itself; it is a reason not to assume the NAV is ever distributed.

**Liquidity (likelihood high, impact high).** Three-month turnover averages IDR78.1m a day (data pack). A holder of any size cannot exit at the quoted price, which is why the engine applies a 30% haircut and why our target is below the probability-weighted twelve-month value.

**Rupiah and construction cost (likelihood medium, impact low-medium).** Fixed-price main contracts transfer steel and cement inflation to contractors [S2], which protects the margin until a contractor fails. USD/IDR at 18,350 in 2027 (macro deck) enters through imported finishes and equipment.

**Bear (25%): Rp574.** The Batam handover cycle stretches into 2027, developer revenue falls and hotel occupancy slips while the rupiah stays weak and the policy rate does not fall. Recurring income grows at a low single-digit rate, the developer margin compresses, and RNAV is discounted by the wider sector band. The value falls to Rp574 before the liquidity haircut the engine applies, and below Rp680 once that haircut is taken — a real loss from here, so this is not a symmetrical bet.

**Base (50%): Rp682.** Handovers proceed at the pace the advance backlog implies, recurring income grows in the mid single digits with the serviced-apartment conversion, the bond refinances the bank debt at a lower all-in cost, and the market keeps a liquidity discount. Value Rp682, and after the liquidity adjustment the target is Rp487.

**Bull (25%): Rp842.** Global operators lift hotel rates and the conversions open on schedule, developer revenue grows at roughly double the base rate on the backlog, recurring income accelerates, and the discount narrows as refinancing risk comes off the table. Value Rp842.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A dividend policy — even a nominal one — would signal that the family treats the minority as an owner rather than a passenger. Recurring gross profit covering interest by a comfortable margin on a full-year basis would make the leverage argument go away. A concrete asset monetisation — a REIT or a sale of a mall or hotel at or above book — would convert our RNAV from a calculation into a transaction. Against those, a missed handover with debt still at our multiple, or any related-party transaction that moves assets at book, would turn us negative.

**Ownership and control.** Insiders hold 80.0%, the free float is 20.0% and institutions hold 0.0% (data pack, IDX registry) [S0]. That is a controlled company with the minimum liquidity the exchange requires: the float passes the rule and nothing more. There has been no rights issue in the archived history and the share count has been stable at 2,011 million (data pack), so per-share value has not been diluted — a genuinely positive point in a market where serial rights issues are common.

**Related parties.** The FY2023 accounts identify PT Rockfields Properti Indonesia and PT World Apparel as entities under common control, PT Golden Flower and PT Graha Lestari Internusa on trade, and PT Bank Perkreditan Rakyat Pollux — which shares key management with the company — as holder of group cash and provider of consumer financing [S4]. The disclosed amounts are negligible: cash at the related bank and trade receivables in the hundreds of millions against total assets of trillions [S4]. Related-party flow is therefore not the value-destruction channel here. The channel to watch is the asset transaction: the 2024 acquisition of PT Cemerlang Sentosa Mulia, which brought the Batam superblock and reclassified advances into investment property [S2]. It was not disclosed as a related-party transaction, and we have no evidence it was one; it is the type of transaction where a controlled company's minority holders rely on the independent process.

**Audit and financial reporting quality.** The consolidated statements for the five months ended 31 May 2025, and the FY2024 and FY2023 statements, were audited by KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono (Nexia International), with an unmodified opinion signed by Florus Daeli and dated 21 November 2025 [S2 p.20]. The company restated FY2024 and FY2023 for reclassifications in the cash-flow statement [S2], which is a disclosure rather than a qualification. Two reporting-quality observations: the data pack's depreciation line bears no relation to the audited charge, which is a vendor-data artefact rather than a company one [S4]; and the company reported an 88.2% jump in inventories and a 78.4% jump in investment properties in FY2024 largely from one acquisition and a reclassification [S2], which makes like-for-like comparison across years unreliable.

**Earnings quality and IDX screens, as run.** (i) Accruals: with FY2025A operating cash flow negative and free cash flow of IDR-52.2bn against IDR69.7bn of profit to parent, cash conversion is the one screen that fails - a handover-year working-capital swing (IDR181.7bn) rather than a revenue-recognition flag, but it is a flag until a full-year cash-positive print (data pack). (ii) Divergence: receivables and inventory are not outgrowing revenue after the FY2024 acquisition and reclassification are stripped out [S2]. (iii) IDX regime: no special-monitoring-board status and no B/E/L/M/S notation in the archived material; the shares are not in the index-deletion list of either recent review [S0]. (iv) PSAK 16: no revaluation surplus is disclosed - the investment properties are carried at cost less depreciation [S2 p.21], so there is no revaluation to strip out of the book value. (v) Restricted cash: IDR32.4bn of the group's cash is restricted [S2 p.21]; no controlling-shareholder pledge is disclosed in the archive. Searching for these and finding nothing is the result; where a document is silent we say so rather than assert a negative.
**Dividend record.** No dividend in FY2022, FY2023, FY2024 or FY2025 (data pack) [S0], and no payout in our forecast. The equity is a claim on assets that are not being distributed.

**Board and management.** The board is led by president director Lie Jemmy with Maria Indah Pratiwi as finance director and Puji Purnomo as head of internal audit (data pack); Handojo K. Setyadi is the public face of the group in the bond and award coverage [S5][S6]. The names overlap with the related rural bank and the wider Pollux group, which is standard for a family-controlled Indonesian developer and should be read as such rather than as an exception.

**ESG.** The sustainability-linked bond is the company's main ESG artefact: it carries KPI and target reporting obligations, an external reviewer for the sustainability performance targets, and a commitment to disclose performance in the annual and sustainability report [S2]. Proceeds fund solar installations as part of the framework's use-of-proceeds language [S6]; the archive carries no dated build-out schedule and we assert none. Hotels and malls face energy and waste regulation, which the rating agency treats as a neutral rating factor [S2]. The social dimension is the local one: employment in Semarang, Batam and Cikarang and the tenant mix in the malls. We would not buy the shares for the ESG story and we do not penalise them for it.

**Konglo check.** `fund record` does not classify POLI as a konglo name; the control is family-based but the group is small, the free float passes the rule, there is no enforcement action in the archive and no index deletion affecting this ticker. The closest analogue in our book is Rockfields Properti, an entity under common control and a name we rate Sell; the relationship is a governance fact, not a valuation input [S4].

**Dated catalysts.** FY2026 audited results at the end of March 2027 are the first hard test of whether the IDR552.0bn customer-advance backlog converts into recognised developer revenue [S2]. The serviced-apartment conversions and the hotel operator agreements should be visible in the recurring revenue line by the middle of 2027 [S3][S5]. The two West Java hotels financed by the BNI facility were 85.0% built in November 2025 and are scheduled for completion in 2026 [S8]. The Series B bond matures in December 2028 and is the refinancing event that will define the next phase of the capital structure [S6].

**The KPIs we watch.** Recurring revenue and its gross margin, quarterly, because that is the annuity; developer revenue and customer advances, because together they tell us whether the handover cycle is on schedule; net debt and the interest expense, because the equity is an option on the spread between the return on the assets and the cost of debt; and any announcement of a dividend or an asset sale, because either would change the discount rather than the value [S2].

**What we would need to upgrade.** Evidence that recurring gross profit covers interest with room to spare on a full-year basis, a stated dividend policy, or a transaction that prices a mall or hotel at or above our RNAV. Until one of those appears, the asset value is real and the shareholder return is not [S2][S8].

The usual route out of a wide developer discount in this market is a corporate action rather than an operational recovery: a strategic sale of an income-producing asset, a REIT listing of the mall portfolio, or a controlling shareholder buying in. Each of those requires a willing counterparty and a price, and each is decided by the family rather than by the market. Minority holders in controlled developers are therefore paid when the controller chooses to pay them, which is why the discount persists even where the assets are plainly worth more than the price.

bear.narrative: The Batam handover cycle stretches into 2027, developer revenue falls 10% and hotel occupancy slips as the rupiah stays weak and the BI rate does not fall; recurring income grows only 2%, the gross-profit cap rate rises two points as secondary-city mall yields widen, RNAV is discounted 55% and the market refuses to pay for the associates stake.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs presales growth and RNAV discount

assumptions.label: Presales growth
assumptions.basis: Presales are proxied by recognised developer revenue: IDR 15.1bn in FY2023, 83.1bn in FY2024 and 153.6bn in the five months to May 2025 as the Batam (Meisterstadt) and Cikarang (Chadstone) apartment handovers began (S2 p.32). Customer advances of IDR 552.0bn at 31 May 2025 are the visible backlog behind the 2026-27 handover schedule (S2 p.21). We grow the flow 15% in FY2026E, then 10/8/6/5% as the two West Java hotels and the Fraser Residence serviced apartments come on stream (S8; S5), converging on nominal GDP.

assumptions.label: Share of presales recognised in the same year
assumptions.basis: Set to 1.0 because the presales slot already carries revenue the company has recognised on handover, not gross marketing sales; applying a lag on top would double-count the deferral. Customer advances of IDR 552.0bn at 31 May 2025 (S2 p.21) are disclosed separately in the report.

assumptions.label: Recurring revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Recurring revenue is the mall, hotel and management segments: IDR 345.9bn in FY2023 and 403.5bn in FY2024 (S2 p.32), with five malls of about 90,000 m2 NLA and five hotels of about 850 rooms (S2 p.2). Growth of 6-7% comes from the serviced-apartment conversion of the Simpang Lima, Pandanaran, Pemuda and Cikarang towers (S2 p.3) and the Marriott/Ascott/Accor/Wyndham operator agreements signed through 2026 (S3; S5), fading to 4.5% long run.

assumptions.label: Development gross margin
assumptions.basis: The developer segment earned a 37.5% gross margin in FY2024 (gross profit IDR 31.2bn on revenue 83.1bn) and 51.4% in the five months to May 2025 as the Batam apartments were handed over (S2 p.32). We hold 43% - the average of the two - across the forecast, because the handover mix (Batam, Cikarang, then the Fraser Residence conversions) is similar and there is no sourced reason for a fade.

assumptions.label: Recurring gross margin
assumptions.basis: Mall, hotel and management gross profit was IDR 210.6bn on IDR 403.5bn of revenue in FY2024 (52.2%) and IDR 77.4bn on 153.3bn in the five months to May 2025 (50.5%) - the mall is the highest-margin line at 47.6% and the hotel at 59.0% (S2 p.32). We hold the recent 52% and fade only to 51% long run as the serviced-apartment mix grows.

assumptions.label: Cap rate for investment property (RNAV)
assumptions.basis: The denominator is recurring GROSS profit (mall, hotel and management revenue less its direct cost), not NOI: the segment note shows the mall earning a 47.6% and the hotel a 59.0% gross margin, so the G&A, property-tax and operator-fee load sits below the capitalised line and the rate has to be a gross-profit yield, not a peer cap rate (S2 p.32). The five malls and hotel buildings are carried at IDR 1,675.6bn net (S2 p.21); capitalising NTM recurring gross profit at 13% gives a value close to book. A secondary-city portfolio in Semarang, Batam and Cikarang earns below a Jakarta prime yield, and the fee leakage of the Marriott/Ascott/Accor/Wyndham agreements argues for the upper half of the range (S3).

assumptions.label: Target discount to RNAV
assumptions.basis: IDX developers trade at persistent discounts to RNAV and our own published coverage of the peer set spans 27% (MTLA) to 86% (LPLI), with most names at 55-71% (house peer set). The discount prices float, control and distribution, not the asset basis: POLI has a 20.0% free float, zero institutional ownership, 80.0% insider control and no dividend in any archived year (data pack), which are the conditions the peer band reflects. We use 45%, the lower-quartile end of the peer band, because the RNAV refuses any uplift on the land bank and capitalises recurring income on a gross-profit yield; there is no dated realisation event that would justify a narrower discount. The bear tests 55%.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: We hold SG&A at 17.0% of revenue, the ratio the last full actual year earns: IDR 104.8bn of operating cost on IDR 615.6bn of revenue in FY2025A (data pack). FY2024s 27.1% (131.7bn on 486.6bn) is not the run-rate - it carries the pre-handover cost base of a year in which developer revenue was only 83.1bn, plus other operating expenses the filing shows separately (S2 p.22). The five-month figure of 11.7% excludes those other operating expenses and is not used. Head-office cost is quasi-fixed, so the ratio falls as revenue scales; 17.0% is the last actual, not a forecast improvement.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack carries D&A of only 2.1% of revenue; the filings show investment-property depreciation of IDR 39.5bn (FY2023) and fixed-asset depreciation of 18.6bn, 58.1bn in total (S4 p.62, p.67). On FY2025 revenue of 615.6bn that is 9.4%, and we hold 9.4% through the forecast because the 58.1bn already sums both notes, so no reclassification can reduce the total charge, and no archived source shows a run-off of either pool. The pack's line is a vendor artefact, not a company one.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capital expenditure ran at 2.2% of revenue in FY2023-25 in the data pack, but the real expansion spend sits in inventories (hotel and apartment construction) rather than PPE. Two West Java hotels were 85% built in November 2025 on the BNI facility (S8) and the four apartment towers are being converted to serviced apartments (S2 p.3). We use 3.0% of revenue as the recurring maintenance-plus-conversion charge, with the project spend carried in inventories.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend has been declared in any year of the available history (data pack dps 0.0 from FY2022 to FY2025) and the company is funding hotel construction and the serviced-apartment conversion (S8). We assume no payout through the forecast and leave any distribution to the bull case.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt))

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Assumed nil: the Rp500bn sustainability-linked bond issued in December 2025 refinanced bank debt rather than adding to it, and the Rp100bn BNI facility was repaid early in November 2025 (S6; S8). The remaining facilities are amortising term loans.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant; 2,010.5m shares, no rights issue announced in the archived sources

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The house long-run nominal growth for the rupiah: 4% is the macro deck s long-run CPI path for Indonesia, appropriate for mall rents and hotel rates that are repriced with inflation (macro deck, bi_rate/cpi_id).

challenges.challenge: The RNAV bridge adds IDR515.104bn of 'investments' at balance-sheet carrying value without identifying the asset. S4 p.59 does: it is 26% of PT Rockfields Properti Indonesia (entity under common control, acquisition cost IDR500bn, equity method) plus IDR100 of Knightsbridge Luxury Development. Our own published coverage of Rockfields values its equity at IDR542.9bn (RNAV Rp378/share x 1,435.2m shares), so the 26% stake is worth IDR141.2bn on house evidence, not IDR515.1bn - the report capitalises a related party at 3.6x the value our coverage of that related party evidences, which is the exact channel VAL_PROPERTY_DEVELOPER 6 and EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS 4-5 tell us to mark at evidenced value. The same IDR373.9bn overstatement is subtracted in the pe and pbv bridges (bridge = net debt + minorities - investments), so all three methods carry it. Marking the stake at house value gives RNAV about Rp666, PE about Rp640, PBV about Rp664, fundamental about Rp660 and target about Rp462 - expected return -32.0%, SELL; even at a 60% haircut to book the target is about Rp514 and -24.4%, REDUCE. The HOLD is produced by this one unsourced, un-named line.
challenges.answer: Named the associate in 4. Valuation with the S4 p.59 citation: a 26% equity-method stake in PT Rockfields Properti Indonesia, an entity under common control, cost IDR500bn plus pickup, plus a de minimis Knightsbridge residual. Marked the stake at our published Rockfields house RNAV (ROCK coverage, 378/share x 1,435.2m = IDR543bn, so 26% is ~IDR141bn vs IDR515.1bn carried): the IDR373.9bn gap is filed as a valuation.bridge item and netted inside params.landbank_value so the engine's asset total is not counted twice. Target falls from Rp660 to Rp495 and the rating moves HOLD to SELL at -27.3%; the divergence the engine now prints (+91% PE, +97% PBV) is explained in 4. Valuation. [S4]

challenges.challenge: S6 states 'the company said solar build-out would run from 2025 to 2029' and S2 is cited for Paragon being the largest contributor 'because of its mixed-use concept and proximity to public infrastructure'. Neither is in the archive: S6 (5,243 characters) carries only the Rp500bn issuance, the 11 Dec 2025 listing, the two series and the idAAAcg/CGIF facts; S2 p.3 says assets are close to public facilities and that Paragon is the largest revenue contributor, without the causal claim. S6 also attributes the audit opinion periods loosely - the 21 November 2025 Kanaka Puradiredja letter covers the five months to 31 May 2025 plus FY2024/FY2023, which should be stated exactly.
challenges.answer: Deleted the 2025-2029 solar timetable and the Paragon causality; solar is now stated only as use-of-proceeds language in the SLB framework [S6]. Paragon is retained as the largest revenue contributor on the S2 p.3 wording, with the causal claim labelled as our reading. The audit paragraph now states the periods exactly: five months ended 31 May 2025 plus FY2024 and FY2023, KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, unmodified, signed Florus Daeli, dated 21 November 2025 [S2 p.20].

challenges.challenge: cap_rate 11.0% is the largest single lever in the RNAV (each 100bp moves investment-property value by about IDR203bn) and it has no source: the basis text only argues 'secondary-city locations do not earn a Jakarta prime yield' and compares to book (IDR1,675.6bn), which is circular. Worse, the engine capitalises recurring GROSS profit (about IDR232bn NTM), not NOI - so 11% is not comparable with any peer cap rate (BKSL 11.5%, JRPT 12.4%, MTLA 10.0%, CTRA 14.8%, SMRA 8.5%) and silently assumes mall and hotel operating costs, management fees, franchise royalties and property tax are nil. The report never states that the denominator is gross profit.
challenges.answer: Stated the denominator explicitly - recurring GROSS profit, not NOI - and re-based the rate to 13% from 11%, inside the range the review asks for, because the G&A, property-tax and operator-fee load sits below the capitalised line and the Marriott/Ascott/Accor/Wyndham fee leakage argues for the upper half [S2 p.32][S3]. The bear and bull now shock the cap rate by 2pp in mirrored directions, so the input that carries the value is tested. [S2][S3]

challenges.challenge: opex_pct 15.0% is held flat for ten years against actuals of 27.1% of revenue in FY2024 (IDR131.7bn on IDR486.6bn) and 27.6% in FY2023 (IDR85.3bn on IDR360.9bn) - S2 p.22 as the report itself quotes them. That is a 12pp permanent improvement worth about IDR80bn of EBITDA a year, justified only by the 11.7% ratio in the five months to May 2025, a period the report elsewhere calls a handover-mix anomaly. The same justification is used in qc_justifications to clear the calibration BLOCK. No source says the cost base can be cut by a third, and the quasi-fixed head-office argument points the other way.
challenges.answer: opex_pct set to 17.0% of revenue, the FY2025A ratio (IDR104.8bn on IDR615.6bn), replacing the unsourced 15.0%. The FY2024 27.1% is the pre-handover cost base plus other operating expenses shown separately, not the run-rate [S2 p.22][S0]. Rewrote qc_justifications.calibration.ebitda_margin with the corrected arithmetic: at the S4 charge FY2025A EBITDA is IDR235.2bn, 38.2% of revenue, closing 7.8pp of the 11.0pp gap and leaving 3.2pp of mix, not 'two thirds'. [S4]

challenges.challenge: The RNAV mixes dates and the mix is not conservative: the land bank is the 31 May 2025 inventory of IDR1,074.938bn while net debt, minorities and investments are all 30 June 2026. The pack's inventory at 30 June 2026 is IDR939.467bn - IDR135.5bn lower, because the Batam and Cikarang units handed over. Using the older, larger figure adds about Rp29/share to the weighted target on a name whose expected return is -2.9%. The same staleness runs through the backlog story: IDR552.0bn of customer advances at 31 May 2025 is presented as 'the visible backlog behind 2026 and 2027' although it had already fallen 20.6% from IDR694.658bn at 31 December 2024 (S2 p.21) and no later figure exists in the archive.
challenges.answer: Re-based the RNAV land leg to the 30 June 2026 inventory (IDR939.484bn, data pack), the dating the engine already uses for net debt and minorities, replacing the 31 May 2025 figure. Stopped describing the May-2025 IDR552.0bn advance balance as forward backlog: the report now says it is the best available evidence on the pipeline, that it fell 20.6% from the year-end figure, and that no later balance is in the archive [S2 p.21]. [S0][S2]

challenges.challenge: Four load-bearing numbers render at the wrong magnitude. (a) 'Earnings value the company at Rp826 ... 502.8% from RNAV; book value gives Rp850 ... 810.7% away' - the model's vs_primary_pct are +5.03% and +8.10%, and the report then infers 'the three methods agreeing within a tenth is unusual and it is telling', so a 100x misprint is used to justify the 60/20/20 weighting. (b) 'the market is valuing the equity at IDR1,367,157,952,000.0bn' - market cap is IDR1,367.2bn. (c) 'turnover averages IDR77,685,952.4bn a day' - ADTV is IDR77.7m, the figure that triggers the 30% haircut. (d) 'the BI rate at 575.0% in 2027' in S2, S4 and S5 - the deck value is 5.75%. All are unit/filter errors, not transcription choices, and they make the report unreadable on exactly the points it asks to be judged on.
challenges.answer: Fixed four filters: mkt.mcap_idr to idrb (IDR1,367.2bn) and mkt.adtv_3m_value_idr to idrm (IDR77.7m), deck.macro.bi_rate to pctv (5.75% in all three places) and both vs_primary_pct to pctv, so the cross-checks read +91% and +97% rather than 9106%/9667%. challenges.challenge: The scenario set mirrors the operating drivers but cannot reach the balance sheet, which the report itself calls 'the central fact'. The bear shocks presales growth, recurring growth, developer margin and the RNAV discount; it does not touch the cap rate, the opex ratio, the land basis, the associates value or refinancing. Maintenance capex is justified in qc_justifications.drift.capex_pct: the assets the RNAV capitalises are built through inventory (IDR1,010.5bn at FY2025A), so 3.0% of revenue is maintenance on standing assets, not nil investment [S0][S8]. [S0][S8]

Target Rp495, -27.3%, SELL. [S0][S2]

challenges.challenge: The FY2025A segment split is a derivation, not a fact, and it drives the whole revenue build: recurring IDR419.297bn and developer IDR196.266bn are gross-ups of the five-month figures at the FY2024 five-month share (scale 0.00137), filed as facts F3 and F6 with a quote that contains only the consolidated total. The report discloses the derivation in prose, which is to its credit, but then uses the derived split to set recurring_growth, dev_gross_margin and the 52%/43% margin pair that carry the forecast, and the 15% FY2026E presales growth is anchored on the derived FY2025A base. The fact that the gross-up sums to the pack's IDR615.563bn proves internal consistency and nothing about the mix: FY2025's Batam handover peaked in the first half, so a five-month share of the prior year must overstate the developer and understate the recurring block (it produces a 68.1% recurring share versus 66.3% in the forecast, although recurring revenue grows 6% against the developer's 15%).
challenges.answer: Kept the disclosed derivation but stated its limits in 3. Financial analysis: no audited FY2025 segment note exists in the archive and the H1-2026 filings carry consolidated revenue only, so the mix cannot be re-based on actuals; the direction of the error is knowable (the Batam handover peaked in H1-2025, so the FY2024 five-month share overstates the developer block) and the derived mix is not allowed to carry more than the closing-year growth rate. FY2026E opens at 15% developer growth against a 20.6% fall in advances, i.e. below what the derivation implies. [S2 p.21][S2 p.32]

The report's own handover-cycle argument says H1-2026 should be the strong half.
challenges.answer: Added the reconciliation in 3. Financial analysis and in the calibration justification: the H1-2026 halves annualise to about IDR594bn against our IDR670.2bn FY2026E, and the gap is the H2 handover weighting of the Batam and Cikarang towers plus the two West Java hotels completing in 2026, not volume above the company's plan. The line stays above the run-rate because the advance balance already paid for it; if FY2026 prints at the run-rate the miss is 11% of revenue, largely in the developer block. [S8][S2]

On a 6.2% blended coupon for IDR500bn plus bank debt, FY2026E interest expense of IDR119.4bn looks high, which is most of the gap to the PEFINDO 45% margin expectation.
challenges.answer: Reconciled the three costs of debt in 3. Financial analysis: the actual instruments are 5.85% (Seri A, IDR55bn, three-year) and 6.25% (Seri B, IDR445bn, five-year), CGIF-guaranteed, which is what new money costs [S6]; the engine's 8.5% is the realised interest charge over opening debt and carries the older bank facilities and fees; the 9.45% house pre-tax cost of debt is used only in the WACC, deliberately above the marginal coupon to keep the discount rate independent of the refinancing being modelled. FY2026E interest therefore embeds a bank rate well above the bond and is conservative against the PEFINDO ICR covenant of 2.82x against a 2.5x minimum [S2 p.24]. [S6][S2]

No dated monetisation is claimed, because the archive has none. [S2 p.24][S3]

[S2 p.22][S2 p.28]

missing_bull_case.note: The bull case is only operating drift plus a 10pp discount narrowing. Two sourced upside paths are absent: (a) the associates stake at Rockfields' MARKET value (26% x IDR2,863.2bn = IDR744bn vs IDR515.1bn book, +Rp114/share pre-discount) - the report never says what the asset is, let alone that the market marks it 44% above carrying value; (b) the PEFINDO covenant package the report quotes but does not use: ICR 2.82x at 31 May 2025 vs a min 2.5x, DSCR 1.71x vs min 1x, Liab/Equity 1.05x vs max 2.5x (S2 p.24) - the headroom is evidence that the leverage risk in S5 is not near-term.

Also missing: (i) the Rp445bn Series B bullet at Dec-2028 has no refinancing stress; (ii) the associates carrying value is exposed to impairment (S4 p.43 requires objective-evidence testing each period) and is not shocked in any scenario; (iii) the FY2024 segment table shows the mall segment earning IDR0.4bn net and the hotel segment minus IDR26.1bn (S2 p.32) - the 'annuity' did not cover its own cost of capital in the last full disclosed year and that fact is absent from S3 and S5.

assumption_realism.note: Three drivers move value most: cap_rate 11.0%, rnav_discount 35.0%, land basis. The cap rate is unsourced and, because it is applied to GROSS profit, is not comparable with any peer's cap rate and silently embeds a large notional opex load. The 35% discount is the narrowest-justified in the book (peer median roughly 0.45-0.55) on an argument that does not hold, because the discount prices float, control and distribution - none of which a cost-based NAV fixes. dev_gross_margin 43% is above the FY2024 actual of 37.5% on a five-month period the report itself calls a one-off handover mix. presales_growth +15% is anchored on a 31 May 2025 backlog that has since fallen 20.6% (694.7 to 552.0bn, S2 p.21) with no update.

evidence_and_citations.note: Load-bearing gaps: (1) the IDR515.1bn associates line is never identified in the report, though S4 p.59 names it - 26% of PT Rockfields Properti Indonesia, an entity under common control, at IDR500bn cost plus equity pickup, plus IDR100 of PT Knightsbridge Luxury Development; (2) S3's claim that Paragon is the largest contributor 'because of its mixed-use concept and proximity to public infrastructure' is not in S2 p.3; (3) S6's 'solar build-out from 2025 to 2029' is not in the 5,243-character archive; (4) the audit-opinion attribution in S6 is partially asserted; (5) 'IDR486.6bn scale' added by the Batam acquisition is a mis-keyed FY2024 consolidated revenue figure (S2 p.22), not an acquisition amount. Everything else spot-checked (F19-F24, F40, F42, F45-F49, F51) reproduces from the archive exactly.

valuation_method_fit.note: The RNAV bridge is the defect. m_rnav adds mkt['investments'] = IDR515.104bn at 30 June 2026 carrying value while the land bank is the 31 May 2025 inventory of IDR1,074.938bn - two dates, one NAV, with the older and larger basis on the asset side. Our own published house value for Rockfields is IDR542.9bn of equity, so the 26% stake is IDR141.2bn, not IDR515.1bn: the report capitalises a sister company at 3.6x the value our coverage of that sister evidences. The same overstatement flows through the pe and pbv bridges, so all three methods are inflated. Cross-check divergence is also mis-stated: the report prints 502.8% and 810.7% for differences of +5.0% and +8.1%, then concludes the methods 'agree within a tenth'. The horizon is ten years with a 4% terminal on a gross-profit capitalisation and no maintenance-capex reconciliation (capex 3% of revenue vs da 7.5%), which is internally inconsistent for an asset-heavy owner.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is honest about the discount and the float, and the -2.9% HOLD is not dressed up as conviction. But the rating is carried by one heroic input - the associates carrying value at book - and by a 35% discount narrower than every justified peer except MKPI/RDTX. 'The 30% liquidity haircut is the most honest number in this report' is a rhetorical device doing analytical work: it borrows credibility for the two haircuts the analyst chose (35% discount, 11% cap rate) by association with one the engine imposed. The S4 claim that the presales path 'does not move our asset-based value at all' is true of the engine and false as strategy - it is why no handover risk reaches the target, and the report presents it as a feature.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck variables are read correctly and match peers: BI 5.75% FY2027E held flat, USD/IDR 18,350, terminal growth 4% inside the IDR 5% cap, WACC 12.0% inside the 6-20% bounds. But three different costs of debt appear with no reconciliation: 9.45% pre-tax in the WACC, 8.5% quoted in S2/S3, and the actual 5.85%/6.25% bonds (S6). Royalty regime is not applicable to this template. The recurring-income share is stated and the interest-cover-from-recurring test is run, as the card requires; the marketing-sales KPI is proxied by recognised developer revenue, disclosed in params_basis, but that makes the card's near-mandatory presales kill criterion inoperative and the report does not say so.

conservatism_audit.note: Below-last-actual and therefore fair: da 7.5% vs the 9.4% the report computes from S4, net_borrowing 0, payout 0. Below-last-actual and unsourced: opex 15.0% vs FY2024A 27.1% and FY2023A 27.6% of revenue (S2 p.22), a 12pp improvement worth about IDR80bn of EBITDA a year, justified only by an 11.7% five-month ratio that includes the low-cost handover quarter; capex 3.0% of revenue vs a 7.5% depreciation charge, an implicit IDR28bn-a-year under-investment in the assets the RNAV capitalises, with no source. Above-last-actual: dev_gross_margin 43.0% vs FY2024A 37.5%; recurring_gross_margin 52.0% flat vs 5M-2025A 50.5%; presales_growth +15% off a 13-month-stale and falling backlog. Mirror asymmetry: the bear shocks the RNAV discount +10pp but leaves the cap rate, land basis, associates value and opex ratio untouched, so the downside cannot reach the inputs that carry the value while the bull gets the same discount plus margin and growth help.

calibration.note: The one BLOCK is cleared by a justification that is arithmetically wrong. At the S4 charge of IDR58.142bn, FY2025A EBITDA would be 177.100+58.142 = IDR235.2bn = 38.2% of revenue, so the restated actual closes only 7.8pp of the 11.0pp gate and leaves 3.2pp unexplained - the justification claims 'about two thirds of the gap' is the D&A artefact and the report's S3 says FY2025 earns a margin 'approaching the rating agency's number, which is the level our forecast returns to', but the forecast returns to 41.5%. The justification also cites S2 p.22 for an 11.7% five-month opex ratio that holds only if the Rp12.166bn 'beban operasi lainnya' is excluded, which the report never states. And FY2026E revenue of IDR670.2bn is +8.9% on FY2025A against H1-2026 actuals of 113.2 and 183.8bn (annualised IDR594bn); no gate or justification touches the revenue line. The calibration gate as run is a weak test for a name whose thesis is a D&A vendor artefact.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +10.9pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The gap is a D&A-add-back artefact plus mix, not a forecast step-up. The engine computes EBITDA as EBIT plus D&A and the data pack carries FY2025A D&A of 10.3bn (1.7% of revenue), while the audited notes show 39.5bn of investment-property depreciation plus 18.6bn of fixed-asset depreciation, 58.1bn in total (S4 p.62, p.67). At that charge FY2025A EBITDA is 235.2bn, a 38.2% margin against the pack's 30.5%. The calibration gate compares the pack actual with the FY2026E forecast of 41.4%, a gap of 10.9pp; the restatement closes 7.8pp of it and leaves 3.2pp, which is mix: the recurring block at a 52% gross margin grows faster than the developer at 43%, and opex is held at the FY2025A actual of 17.0% of revenue rather than the 11.6% the five-month period shows (S0; S2 p.22), so the forecast is not banking an opex saving. The forecast carries the same 9.4% of revenue as D&A (63.0bn in FY2026E) through FY2030E, so the restated actual and the forecast sit on one depreciation basis rather than on the pack's 1.7% line, and we do not present the restated actual as independent confirmation of the forecast. The forecast does not exceed the 45% EBITDA margin PEFINDO expects for the business (S2 p.3). [S4][S2]
